Print a fitted model

Source: R/model-classes.R, R/model-rf.R
print.spatial_fit.Rd

Prints the backend, the formula, the number of observations and the CRS, then lines for the backend:

  • a random forest (rf_fit): the number of trees, mtry, the node size, whether the coordinates were used as predictors, how each tree's rows were sampled, the out-of-bag error and the largest importances. A forest fitted without them prints "no spatial information used": it sees the covariates alone. One fitted with include_coords = TRUE prints a note on how to score it (see "Coordinates as predictors" and "Out-of-bag error" in fit_rf_model()). When a predictor is an unordered factor or a character column, a line says how ranger was told to split it;

  • a GWR (gwr_fit): the bandwidth (a count of neighbours, or a distance with the CRS's unit), the kernel, the AICc, the effective number of parameters and, when any local window is of deficient rank, the number of such windows;

  • a Bayesian GP (bayesian_fit): the GP basis size, the smallest effective range the basis resolves in CRS units, the LOOIC when the fit computed it (compute_loo = TRUE, the default of fit_bayesian_spatial_model()), the slope prior, the standardised predictors, and a flagged line when the sampler's diagnostics or the basis check failed.

A custom subclass prints the common lines only. Typing the object's name calls this method; use it to confirm that a fit used the data, predictors and CRS you meant. For fit quality use model_metrics() or summary.spatial_fit(). Apart from a forest's out-of-bag error and a Bayesian GP's LOOIC, an approximate leave-one-out score of single rows, nothing printed here is an out-of-sample score, and neither of those is a spatial one.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'spatial_fit'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'rf_fit'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

x

A spatial_fit object.

...

Not used.

Value

x, invisibly.

See also

fit_rf_model(), fit_gwr_model() and fit_bayesian_spatial_model(), which make the objects.

Other fit methods: plot.spatial_fit(), spatial_fit-coef, spatial_fit-fitted, spatial_fit-predict, spatial_fit-residuals, summary.spatial_fit()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(60, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(60, 0, 1000),
             a = rnorm(60)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
pts$z <- 10 + 2 * pts$a + rnorm(60, 0, 0.3)
fit <- fit_rf_model(pts, "z", "a", num_trees = 50, seed = 1)
fit                     # print.rf_fit()
#> <Random Forest (ranger)> spatial model fit
#>   Formula : z ~ a
#>   n       : 60
#>   CRS     : EPSG:32632
#>   Trees   : 50 (mtry = 1, min node = 5)
#>   Coords as predictors: no - no spatial information used; see ?fit_rf_model
#>   Sampling: bootstrap, with replacement (100.0% of rows per tree)
#>   OOB RMSE: 0.4094   OOB R^2: 0.9502
#>   Importance (permutation): a=6.034
#> 
#>   OOB is a random hold-out: under spatial autocorrelation it is the error
#>   of predicting among the samples, and reads low for predictions made
#>   farther from the data than the samples sit from each other. Score a map
#>   that predicts farther with cv_rf() on folds at its distances
#>   (?fold_separation).
if (requireNamespace("sp", quietly = TRUE))
  print(fit_gwr_model(pts, "z", "a", bandwidth = 30))   # print.spatial_fit()
#> <GWR> spatial model fit
#>   Formula : z ~ a
#>   n       : 60
#>   CRS     : EPSG:32632
#>   Bandwidth: 30 neighbours (adaptive, bisquare kernel)
#>   AICc    : 47.44
#>   Eff. parameters: 13.2 of 60 observations
